description: Recon Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Cl0p - Til You Drop - 6 years, 9 Campaigns, 7 0Days
talks.teaser: Maps the infrastructure behind Cl0p's exploitation campaigns, from hosting and ASN reuse to reconnaissance that preceded some attacks by years.
talks.summary:
Speaker Eli Woodward, a threat intelligence advisor at Team Cymru, reviews the exploitation campaigns attributed to the Cl0p group since 2020. The group has repeatedly targeted managed file transfer products and other edge devices that hold large volumes of data, from Accellion through MOVEit to CentreStack. The campaign count changed between the submission and the event as new activity surfaced.

The middle of the talk focuses on infrastructure. Drawing on prior vendor reporting, passive DNS and hosting records, the presenter built a lookup tool that links IP addresses and ASNs to specific campaigns. One hosting provider appears across several campaigns, only about a third of ASNs were ever reused, and some scanning traced back roughly two years before exploitation. Half of the campaigns landed in the fourth quarter, and recent extortion emails arrived months after data theft, suggesting the group now favors quiet exfiltration over encryption.

The closing advice is practical. Teams should baseline normal traffic on file transfer appliances and treat them as production honeypots, alert on unfamiliar URIs, and limit web application firewall rules to required endpoints with default deny. Organizations should also shorten retention of sensitive files on these systems and share indicators from incident response, since publicly reported IPs were scarce for much of this research.

talks.title: CyberKB When Your AI Copilot Runs Recon, Crawls the Dark Web, & Maps Kill Chain
talks.teaser: Presents CyberKB, a proof-of-concept recon platform where an AI agent named Keke drives offensive tools over a searchable knowledge base of scan data.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with a problem familiar to penetration testers: engagements produce large volumes of noisy scan output, and teams often follow only two or three attack paths before writing a report. They present CyberKB, a proof-of-concept platform, and its language-model assistant Keke, which runs tools against ingested data. They argue that a retrieval knowledge base becomes necessary once an environment reaches very large asset counts, since flat Markdown files stop scaling.

The middle of the talk covers the architecture. Several cooperating agents handle a copilot role, goal monitoring, campaign tasks and an observer that retries failed steps. The platform ingests historical DNS and certificate records, sets up missing tools or writes its own scripts when there is no internet access, and can spread scanning across cloud instances. The speakers said the tool was tested on a Hack the Box machine, taking about six hours to reach an initial foothold and roughly twelve hours to finish, and on a prompt-injection CTF. They also described self-adjusting prompts with a human approval step, and admitted that smaller local models give inconsistent tool calls and that techniques missing from the knowledge base cause failures.

The main takeaway for practitioners is the idea of keeping all collected recon data searchable so earlier findings are reused rather than lost, and of treating model-driven output as something to validate. The talk is framed as a proof of concept rather than a product, and the accuracy and performance figures were given without independent benchmark data.

talks.title: InQuorigible - Quora in Missing Persons OSINT
talks.teaser: Shows how Quora keeps deleted questions, activity logs and banned-user traces visible to anyone who knows a username, useful for OSINT investigators.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who volunteered on a missing persons investigation, looks at Quora as an OSINT source. The site runs on natural-language questions that draw in a young, less tech-savvy audience. Moderation is mostly automated, user-owned spaces are not bound by the same disclosure rules as main-site answers, and accounts are easy to register, flip or replace. The talk argues that this combination shapes who uses the site and how they can be found.

The central section covers what stays visible after a user removes content. Deleting a question or limiting a post often leaves the title, slug and author reachable through the public log, activity tab and page source. Follower and following lists, edit history and comment types can help rebuild the shape of an interaction even when the words are gone. Banned accounts keep much of this data visible too. The speaker maps these patterns to OWASP API3 and CWE categories, arguing that exposure of deleted personal content fits CWE-359 better than the broader CWE-200.

The closing part asks the OSINT community to treat Quora as a target in its own right, to report such exposures to the platform and to child-safety reporting channels, and to build better tooling. The speaker shares a bibliography on GitHub and a small username-check tool, and invites collaboration on deeper analysis of the site's JSON responses.

talks.title: Ghost in the Hiring Machine - How to Spot Fake Personas
talks.teaser: Shows how to spot fake job candidates with OSINT, from reverse image searches and public records to document checks and personal privacy hygiene.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the risk of fake remote hires. The speakers describe a 2024 KnowBe4 case where a candidate using a stolen US identity and an AI-enhanced photo passed four video interviews, then had a laptop shipped to a laptop farm that let an overseas operator work from inside the country. Job-market pressure and deepfake tools make such personas easier to build.

The middle covers techniques and two cases. A European rental fraud involved forged identity documents, which were flagged in the EU's Prado database only after the fact. A second case began with a CV, an email address and a LinkedIn photo. Early searches stalled, but rerunning a reverse image search later found a Facebook profile under a different name, matching the identity an HR investigation had uncovered. The talk also surveys US public records, such as business registries, licensing boards and federal court filings, noting which are paid or restricted.

The closing part covers legal limits, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act, stricter California rules, anti-discrimination concerns and GDPR data minimization, and suggests separating data collection from hiring decisions. Practical checks include reverse image searches, verifying credentials at source, confirming shipping addresses and checking archived team pages. The speakers end by urging attendees to audit their own exposure through private profiles, registry opt-outs, aliases and stripped EXIF data.

talks.title: Groking the Kill Chain
talks.teaser: Shows how to constrain LLM-driven recon agents to fixed binaries, sanitized inputs, and structured outputs so they run reliably against real targets.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with recent incidents where autonomous AI agents deleted databases, exceeded their scope, or disrupted services. The speaker argues that unconstrained models are a poor fit for security work because they map a single short prompt onto a huge space of possible outputs. He presents an alternative he calls agents on rails, where the model never picks its own tools, scope, or stopping point.

The design works as a staged pipeline. User input is limited to domains, hosts, ports, and paths, checked against an allow list, and filtered against bug bounty program scopes pulled from HackerOne and Bugcrowd. Scanners such as subfinder, Nmap, and Nuclei run with arguments the developer fixed in advance, with size caps and timeouts, inside a sandboxed Kubernetes instance. The model only analyzes the raw tool output under tight instructions asking for concise, non-alarmist, structured findings, which also keeps token costs low.

The speaker reports a case study covering about 621 hours of scanning across roughly 500 jobs and 45 agents. Of more than 21,000 tasks, over 99 percent completed, and most of the few failures were tools hanging rather than model errors. The AI cost averaged about 44 cents per scan. His takeaway for practitioners is to treat AI as a feature inside a constrained product, and to ask during threat modeling which guardrails are in place.

talks.title: HACKBOTS - Using Agent Frameworks
talks.teaser: Shows how to build AI pentesting agents from markdown skill files, using a JavaScript analysis workflow and a live hackbot build as the worked example.
talks.summary:
Jason Haddix opens by defining hackbots as offensive security automation, with a focus on dynamic black-box testing such as web application reconnaissance. He describes an agent he built for himself that ran against a bug bounty program over several hours and produced multiple critical findings. Modern agent harnesses now let practitioners define agents as markdown skills instead of writing orchestration code, which lowers the barrier to building them.

The core of the talk is method. Before writing a skill, the team maps the expert workflow out, then splits large methodologies into micro-skills, because models tend to skip steps in long checklists. He walks through a JavaScript analysis skill as the example: downloading inline and external scripts, recovering source maps, mining endpoints and parameters, flagging secrets and dangerous sinks, and documenting frameworks. He also covers context engineering. Turning the process into a checklist ledger, adding a separate review pass that rejects incomplete runs, giving concrete examples of good output, and writing exact tool syntax all reduce invented commands and missed steps. Running several models and repeated runs is recommended because outputs vary between runs.

The session ends with a live build of the skill, which was still underway when time ran out. The practical takeaways are to keep skills small, specify output layout and full tool paths, keep output folders outside skill folders to avoid context rot, and read the reasoning traces to find where an agent fails.

talks.title: Living Off Someone Else's Inference
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers locate exposed LLM inference servers and leaked API keys, validate them, and route agent tooling through them at no cost.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attackers increasingly want someone else's LLM compute, because using their own API keys leaves a billing and identity trail and gets expensive once agent loops run for millions of tokens. The presenters walk through finding exposed inference servers, such as LiteLLM, Ollama and vLLM deployments, with internet search queries, then confirming that an endpoint answers a basic chat request.

A central problem is honeypots. The team describes three patterns they saw: servers that return the same reply no matter the input, canned conversations with no model behind them, and small local models advertised under the names of frontier models. Their tool checks for these and blacklists suspicious hosts, and the speakers say a stronger model-identity check is planned for a later version. They demonstrate pointing a coding agent at a cheap model served from a remote host, and they also show a scanner that finds API keys in a private repository.

They close with a command-and-control agent built on Mythic that delegates post-exploitation tasks to an LLM through existing callbacks. The takeaway for defenders is to lock down inference endpoints and API keys, since exposed compute and credentials give adversaries free, unattributed capacity.

talks.title: OSINT Is Still a Thinking Game - Surviving AI Without Losing Tradecraft
talks.teaser: Explains how reliance on AI erodes OSINT analysts' critical thinking, with real cases of fake imagery and mistranslation and four habits to keep conclusions defensible.
talks.summary:
Niko Dekens, a long-time Dutch government OSINT practitioner, argues that AI will not replace analysts but can wear down their critical thinking. He describes how chatbot answers look convincing yet are often wrong, and how synthetic accounts, fabricated documents and AI-edited images are increasingly seeded so that search engines and language models surface them. The question, he suggests, is no longer only whether a source exists but whether it was made to be found.

He illustrates the risk with examples. Students geolocated an AI-generated Amsterdam street and accepted it without checking a map. A Russian-language Telegram phrase was translated as an imminent attack when it meant the opposite. A sudden drop in shipping volume was read as financial distress until a port strike turned out to explain it. He also covers exposed chat histories that reveal investigative focus, and online grooming that pushes young people toward violence through closed messaging channels.

His defense framework has four habits: read the raw source rather than the summary, force a second hypothesis, separate speed from confidence, and audit dependence by labelling AI-assisted content in reports. The practical takeaway is to keep reasoning visible, verify top results by hand, and ask what evidence would change the conclusion.

talks.title: Recon on Trial - The OSINT Operators Legal Playbook
talks.teaser: Maps common open-source recon tasks, from scraping and subdomain enumeration to API calls, onto their likely criminal and civil legal exposure.
talks.summary:
The talk examines routine open-source reconnaissance tasks, including scraping public sites, enumerating subdomains, searching GitHub for leaked secrets and calling APIs, and asks where each one starts to create legal exposure. The speaker, a court-qualified expert witness with a regulator background, treats three questions separately: is it a crime, can the operator be sued, and how would it look to an employer. Clearing one does not clear the others.

The middle section covers the main statutes. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act hinges on access "without authorization" and "exceeds authorized access", and the Supreme Court's Van Buren ruling narrowed the second phrase. Scraping public pages was found not to violate the CFAA in the LinkedIn dispute, yet contract terms still created liability. The Uber case shows how a bug bounty payout cannot cover a concealed breach, and the person who covered it up went to prison. Passive enumeration sits low on the risk scale, while forced zone transfers or brute forcing move toward active access. Using a discovered API key is where the line is crossed.

The closing section addresses preservation letters, which can arrive before any lawsuit or charge. The advice is to stop activity, delete nothing, avoid talking to investigators and bring in an attorney. Privacy laws such as GDPR and CCPA can still bring statutory damages even when criminal exposure is avoided. The practical takeaway is to stick to public, ungated data, read terms of service, and get explicit written scope before touching anything beyond that. The talk is not legal advice.

talks.title: The Breach is Over - The Exposure is Not
talks.teaser: Tracks how credentials leaked in the Shai-Hulud npm worm campaigns stay usable for months, and what their leftover names reveal about infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Anant Srivastava alone after his co-presenter could not attend, looks past the usual end of a supply chain incident. It describes the two Shai-Hulud npm worm waves, which stole secrets from developer machines and CI systems. The second wave used GitHub as its drop point, reusing tokens from earlier dumps to create new repositories, and roughly 35,000 repositories were tracked. Later campaigns encrypted their uploads to slow down casual copying.

The speaker then reports how long the exposure lasted. From a sample of first-wave repositories, most GitHub tokens were still live close to a year later, and their private repositories had been made the only change. A later verified scan of second-wave data still found about 150,000 active credentials. He also found about 542 working SSH keys across GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab and Hugging Face. Git hosts reveal usernames on SSH login, which makes enumeration easy, and common scanners cover only a few hundred patterns, so self-hosted secrets are missed. Environment variable names such as k8s-prod also disclosed infrastructure details.

A canary AWS credential planted in a decoy repository was used within days. Attacker calls moved from identity checks to targeted queries for models and secrets, with boto3 as the most common user agent. The takeaway is to measure recovery by whether usable exposure disappears, not by whether the original incident is closed. Practitioners should map each credential's blast radius, shorten token lifetimes and cut permissions.

talks.title: There Is No Internet - Cross Domain Recon of all 4 Billion IPv4s
talks.teaser: Shows how cross-referencing registry records, reverse DNS, and service responses across all of IPv4 exposes mismatched and impersonated network infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that IPv4 ownership data is not one trustworthy source. Registration records come from regional registries, reverse DNS names describe what an address claims to be, and the services that answer on an address show what it actually does. The speaker describes how the team scanned the full IPv4 space from temporary cloud virtual machines, then enriched each result with bulk WHOIS data, geolocation, corporate registries, and sanctions lists. Every field was stored with a source date so that results from different scans could be compared over time.

The middle of the talk walks through the anomalies the scans surfaced. Thousands of Iranian addresses were registered to fabricated US street addresses, some copying a real mobile carrier's corporate address. Other Iranian blocks hosted services for Russian platforms, and a cryptocurrency node appeared for about eleven days and then disappeared. Reverse DNS records claimed to be United States government domains, and telecom address space declared in one country geolocated to Los Angeles. The speaker stresses that many of these records are self-reported and unaudited.

The closing point is that a single snapshot misses change. Names, maintainers, and certificates rotated between scans, which showed up only when dated snapshots were compared. For practitioners, the takeaway is to line up several independent sources, decide which fields to trust, and keep provenance notes for every query. The speaker also notes that running this kind of full-space scan is expensive.

talks.title: Total Recon - How We Discovered 1000s of open Agents in The Wild
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers find thousands of exposed AI agents across Copilot Studio, Agent Builder, custom GPTs and MCP servers using enumeration and OSINT.
talks.summary:
The Zenity Labs speakers open by noting that attacks on AI agents already happen in the wild, from agent-to-agent abuse to threat actors probing AI systems for their capabilities. Their focus is how attackers find these agents at all. They argue agents are applications that expose knowledge, tools and identities, so classic attack surface discovery applies, and predictable naming and default settings are the weak points.

For each platform they used a different discovery method. In OpenAI's Agent Builder, starter-kit naming on a hosting platform made subdomains guessable through fuzzing common prefixes and suffixes, and a session secret confirmed a live agent. Hundreds were found, some with sensitive documents. In Microsoft Copilot Studio, agent URLs embed a tenant-linked default environment and a short solution prefix that is often left at its default, which shrinks the search space. Recurring words in agent names then finished the job, yielding thousands of agents. Internet scanning for the MCP session header turned up about 100,000 MCP servers, and backlink searches for embedded Copilot pages found roughly 5,000 agents. Asking agents directly for their tools sometimes worked, and prompt injection got past guardrails the team called soft.

The defender takeaways are to stop relying on obscurity and default names, keep an inventory of public agents, MCP servers and skills, and log agent access so repeated prompts or capability probing show up as discovery signals. The researchers released PowerPwn, an open-source recon tool for testing your own exposure, and said the work maps to OWASP's agentic guidance and MITRE ATLAS. They warned that anything newly public gets probed quickly.

talks.title: Your OpSec Is Showing
talks.teaser: Shows how JARM TLS fingerprints and reused server configurations can cluster adversary infrastructure even after domains and IP addresses change.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that defenders who chase static IP addresses and domains fall behind, because attacker infrastructure rotates quickly while the underlying cryptographic stack tends to persist. The speaker introduces JARM, an active TLS fingerprint that sends ten crafted handshakes with varied cipher orders, protocol versions and extensions, then condenses the server's responses into a 62-character hash. That hash reflects the TLS library in use rather than application content, which makes it useful for spotting shared software choices across hosts.

The middle of the talk works through examples. A widely used public DNS resolver produces a hash shared by a huge number of hosts, so blocking on that hash alone would hit everyone. A raw command-and-control server with a placeholder source address and a default admin port shows how an implementation mistake can make a fingerprint far more telling. The speaker also covers the traps: a legitimate Go-based bakery website matched a C2 signature, and actors using reverse proxies or randomized cipher output can mask the original hash, although the evasion itself can become a new anomaly.

The takeaway is that a JARM match is a strong lead rather than a verdict. Analysts should pair it with certificate names, extension ordering, open port layouts and HTTP response headers, then use those combined filters in internet scanners to find related infrastructure.
